qs.q: A 35-year-old delirious man with fever 39.3°C, BP 70/palpable, a heart murmur, palpable spleen, and splinter hemorrhages is brought to the ED. Most likely lab finding?
qs.e: The clinical picture is acute infective endocarditis. IV drug use is the major risk factor; positive opiate urine screen would confirm this predisposing condition.

qs.q: A neonate has tetany, a heart murmur, serum calcium of 6.3 mg/dL, and a VSD. Over the first year he develops Pneumocystis, Aspergillus, and viral upper respiratory infections. Most likely explanation?
o: Failure of B-cell plasma cell maturation
qs.e: Hypocalcemia (absent parathyroids) + cardiac defects + T-cell deficiency causing fungal and viral infections = DiGeorge syndrome. Chromosome 22q11 deletion causes failure of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouch development → absent thymus and parathyroids.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Heart murmurs are sounds from turbulent blood flow across valves or vessels. They guide clinicians to suspect structural, infectious, or functional cardiac disease. Evaluation integrates history, exam, and targeted tests.

sections.p: A heart murmur is an audible or palpable sound from abnormal blood flow. Diagnosis starts with a focused history, auscultation, and assessment of timing, quality, and radiation.
Severity is graded by intensity, impact on symptoms, and hemodynamic significance. Staging follows valve-specific guidelines (e.g., NYHA for heart failure, ACC/AHA for valve disease).
b: ACC/AHA stage A–D for valve disease

sections.p: Causes range from benign functional murmurs to serious structural lesions. In low‑resource settings, rheumatic heart disease, infective endocarditis, and congenital defects are common.
Patients may be asymptomatic or present with dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, or heart failure. Murmur characteristics often hint at the underlying lesion.
Tests are chosen to answer specific clinical questions. When resources are limited, prioritize bedside tools and simple imaging.

t.b: Normal gradients, no regurgitation; abnormal gradients or regurgitant jets indicate valve disease
Enlarged cardiac silhouette or pulmonary edema suggests heart failure
Positive culture confirms infective endocarditis; negative does not rule it out
Elevated ESR/CRP supports infective or rheumatic processes
Normal wall motion and no effusion reduce urgency; abnormal findings need urgent care

sections.p: Certain features predict rapid deterioration or life‑threatening complications. Prompt recognition can save lives.
b: Unexplained fever, new murmur, or embolic phenomena → endocarditis
Rapidly increasing murmur intensity or new heart failure signs → severe valve dysfunction
New conduction block or arrhythmia → potential for sudden death

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then support cardiac function. Drug choices consider efficacy, safety, and local availability.
b: Diuretics for heart failure (e.g., loop diuretics)
Afterload reducers (ACE inhibitors) for regurgitant lesions

t.b: Avoid nephrotoxic agents if renal function is impaired

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression. Prevention focuses on treating risk factors and early disease.
b: Annual echocardiography for rheumatic heart disease

t.b: Stable parameters suggest no progression; worsening requires intervention

sections.p: Some non‑cardiac conditions mimic murmurs or produce similar symptoms.
Certain tests may give false normals or abnormalities, especially in resource‑limited settings.
b: Low‑grade murmurs may be missed on auscultation
Echocardiography may underestimate regurgitation if image quality is poor
Blood cultures can be negative in early endocarditis

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening dyspnea or chest pain
Signs of embolism (e.g., limb pain, neurological deficits)

faq.q: What is the most common cause of a systolic ejection murmur in adults?
faq.a: Aortic stenosis, often due to calcification or rheumatic disease.

faq.q: Can a murmur be normal in a healthy child?
faq.a: Yes, functional murmurs from increased flow are common and usually benign.

faq.q: When is surgery indicated for a murmur?
faq.a: When the murmur reflects severe valve dysfunction with symptoms or evidence of heart failure.

exam: Describe the approach to a patient with a new systolic murmur and explain how you would differentiate aortic stenosis from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Explain why blood cultures are essential in suspected infective endocarditis and how you would manage a patient with a negative culture but high clinical suspicion.
